newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan devising schemes to securitise loans - sources.
newsitem.headline: Japan devising schemes to securitise loans - sources.

text.p: Japanese banks, brokerages and real estate firms have been working out schemes with the Finance Ministry to securitise problem loans that are backed by real estate collateral, financial industry sources said on Monday.
But they said it may take some time to complete such plans, despite a newspaper report saying the schemes had already been finalised.

"It's still too early to say that we have finalised the schemes," said one financial source. "We have to consider various steps to make the new products popular with investors, and to do so it may take some time to finalise the schemes."

The business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported at the weekend that the Finance Ministry and the securities industry are aiming at the securitisation of 500 billion yen of loans backed by real estate collateral this fiscal year.

The paper also said the new financial products that resulted would be trust certificates with maturities ranging from one to 10 years with higher yields than coupons on bonds issued by Japanese electric power companies.

The paper said the first of these new products could possibly be issued as early as June or July. They would be from problem loans held by Cooperative Credit Purchasing Co Ltd (CCPC), a joint body set up by financial institutions to buy institutions' problem loans.

In March, Japan announced a package of measures aimed at boosting liquidity in its land market. They included an easing of regulations to promote securitisation of collateralised real estate. Those changes affecting trust banks were implemented immediately.

The sources said that to further promote securitisation through the trust banks, the Finance Ministry is expected in June to designate trust certificates on real estate business loans as "securities" under the Securities and Exchange Law. The aim would be to increase liquidity, reliability and investor protection, they said.
The trust certificates would be sold by banks and brokers and be backed by insurance offered by non-life insurance companies, they said.
